one_liner: Multicore CPU SpMV library: CSX compressed format plus LLVM-JIT kernels per matrix; claims parity-or-better vs Intel MKL CSR.
what_it_does: SparseX speeds up repeated sparse matrix-vector products (y = alpha*A*x + beta*y) on Linux SMP and NUMA multicore machines. You load a matrix from CSR arrays or a Matrix Market file, tune it once with spx_mat_tune() into the CSX format, wrap vectors as spx_vector_t objects built from the matrix's thread partition, and call spx_matvec_kernel() in your solver loop. A one-call path, spx_matvec_kernel_csr(), converts CSR on the first call and reuses the tuned handle after that. The C API is its own, not MKL's mkl_sparse_?_mv signature.
how_it_is_fast: SpMV on CPUs is limited by memory bandwidth, and CSR spends one column index per nonzero. CSX (Compressed Sparse eXtended, PPoPP'11 / TPDS'13) detects dense substructures: horizontal, vertical, diagonal and anti-diagonal runs, row- and column-aligned blocks, and delta-encoded leftovers. It stores one short descriptor per substructure instead of per-element indices, which shrinks the index stream. For each matrix, the library fills C kernel templates for the patterns it chose (src/templates/*_tmpl.c), compiles them at runtime with the Clang frontend and LLVM MCJIT, and runs them on a pinned thread pool with NUMA-aware allocation. A symmetric variant (CSX-sym) stores only half the matrix, and optional Reverse Cuthill-McKee reordering improves locality.
when_to_use: Iterative solvers (CG, GMRES, eigen-solvers) on one large sparse matrix that run thousands of SpMVs, so the one-off tuning and JIT cost is amortized; spx_mat_save/spx_mat_restore can skip re-tuning in later runs
Matrices with regular dense substructure (FEM and structural meshes with blocks, diagonals or long row runs), where index compression cuts memory traffic the most
Large symmetric matrices, where CSX-sym (spx.matrix.symmetric) halves the storage that has to be streamed
Multi-socket NUMA Linux servers, where the library's thread pinning and NUMA placement do the tuning for you
As a historical baseline in SpMV research: later papers (DIV, ICS 2025) still benchmark against it
when_not_to_use: One-shot or few SpMVs: the user's guide calls CSX preprocessing (substructure detection plus JIT compile) 'non-negligible' even with sampling

Any current toolchain: configure.ac accepts only LLVM 4.0.0 to 6.0.0, the JIT uses Clang's internal C++ API (which the README says breaks with almost every LLVM release), and the last commit is from 2018. The two open issues (#2 Boost.atomic not found with Boost 1.58, #4 cannot install LLVM) have no fix
Matrices whose sparsity pattern changes: after tuning, nonzeros cannot be inserted or deleted, only existing values updated through spx_mat_set_entry
GPUs, Windows or macOS: CPU only, Linux only (futex wrapper, libnuma required)

When a large margin over MKL is the goal: the only third-party figures found (DIV, ICS 2025, search snippet) put SparseX at a 13% median and 7.7% geometric-mean speedup on large matrices, and DIV reports 1.87x (Intel) and 2.0x (AMD) over SparseX

integration.dependencies: LLVM/Clang 4.0.0-6.0.0 (linked, used at runtime for the JIT), Boost >= 1.48 (atomic, regex, serialization, system), libnuma >= 2.0.7, pthreads; optional Intel MKL or pOSKI for the bundled benchmark driver
integration.min_toolchain: gcc/g++ >= 4.8 plus LLVM/Clang 4.0.0-6.0.0 exactly (configure rejects other versions); autotools (autoreconf -vi) to build from git; JIT kernels are compiled as C99
integration.platforms: Linux on SMP and NUMA multicore CPUs; the JIT targets the host triple, and CPU architectures beyond an x86_64-specific fix in the ChangeLog are not documented
integration.thread_safety: The library runs its own thread pool (spx.rt.nr_threads, default all cores, pinned by spx.rt.cpu_affinity). Calling it concurrently from several user threads is not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — spx_matvec_kernel_csr() accepts plain CSR arrays and computes y = alpha*A*x + beta*y like MKL, but x and y must be wrapped as spx_vector_t objects tied to the matrix partition, and index/value types are fixed at configure time (default int/double)

gotchas: The public headers read (sparsex.h, matvec.h, common.h, types.h) have no extern "C" guards; C++ callers must wrap the #include themselves (the cslab-ntua SpMV-Research wrapper notes undefined references otherwise)
The JIT compiles C at runtime and needs the system C headers: set SPX_JIT_INC_PATH if they are in a non-standard location, and LD_LIBRARY_PATH for a non-standard install prefix

The default thread count and affinity grab all cores with a share-nothing pinning policy, which can clash with an OpenMP or MPI application's own pinning; set spx.rt.nr_threads and spx.rt.cpu_affinity explicitly
The bundled User's Guide still lists LLVM == 3.0, the README says >= 4.0, and configure.ac accepts only 4.0.0-6.0.0; trust configure.ac. Explicit zeros in the input are kept as logical nonzeros
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SparseX over merge-spmv, CSR5 or CVR only when the matrix has strong block, diagonal or run structure (or is symmetric and large) and you can pin an old LLVM 4-6 toolchain. For irregular or scale-free matrices, CVR and merge-spmv report clearer wins over MKL, and SPC5 is the maintained block-kernel option for AVX-512 and ARM SVE.
verified_claims_summary: No SparseX-versus-MKL numbers could be read from an opened page. Per search snippets, the TOMS 2018 abstract claims superior performance on large-scale problems and performance comparable to Intel MKL and ViennaCL. A third-party ICS 2025 paper (DIV, snippet only) says SparseX reliably speeds up SpMV on large matrices by a 13% median and 7.7% geometric mean; its baseline is presumably MKL CSR but is not stated in the snippet, and no hardware or compiler is given.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-06-10, when the last change added LLVM 6 support; BSD-3-Clause and copyable, but expect to port the Clang-based JIT before it builds against any LLVM newer than 6.
sources_read: WebSearch snippets: SparseX TOMS 2018 abstract; DIV: An Index & Value compression method for SpMV on large matrices (ICS 2025)
